title: Leadership Hart, Nick Not Everyone Needs an Action Plan
author: Hart, Nick
summary: Hart argues that action plans are the artifact of the middle layer of school improvement -- the layer that explicitly attempts change -- but two other layers (habitual practice and horizon thinking) are better served by different artifacts. At the habit layer, leaders are better served by a timeline organizing recurring responsibilities. The article provides four planning meeting scenarios, arguing that Scenario 4 (going deep on one or two subjects per meeting) turns a logistics meeting into genuine professional development. At the innovation layer, the artifact is not a plan but freedom, encouragement, connection to like-minded colleagues, and support for getting ideas out of someone's head into reality.
points: * Action planning is the artifact of the middle layer of school improvement and applying it to the habit layer or innovation layer produces the wrong results. * Coherence to a set of principles is usually more important than consistency of practice: when solving the problems of teaching, coherence of principle beats uniformity of method. * Scenario 4 planning meetings -- going deep on one or two subjects -- convert a logistics meeting into professional development, where teachers rehearse tricky explanations, predict misconceptions, and prepare worked examples. * Most teacher learning is informal, happening in conversation while going about day-to-day work, which makes the quality of planning meetings disproportionately important. * At the innovation layer, the agency you want to encourage will be stifled by action planning: what people need is freedom, encouragement, and support for getting an idea into reality.
quotes: Action planning is the artefact of the school improvement layer and systems and processes are far more important artefacts at the habit layer.
Coherence to a set of principles trumps consistency of practice.

The Head of Year selects one or two subjects to look at in detail. The team is encouraged to challenge and adapt elements of the plans. They rehearse tricky explanations. They predict the likely misconceptions that will arise.
Most teacher learning is informal, happening as we go about our day to day work. Not in formal courses or twilight INSET sessions but in conversation with each other.
By mapping out in advance the strategic focuses for team teaching over the year, we can help to bring focus and help the team to have more productive conversations.
We're also susceptible to the trap of the imagined school so the Head of Year getting out and about in the team is important and needs to be planned for.
The agency we want to encourage in this kind of work will be stifled by action planning. We want people to take something that they care about and try something interesting; to break the mould.
